title: Taxpayer First Act
official_summary:
Taxpayer First Act

This bill revises requirements for the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) regarding its organizational structure, customer service, enforcement procedures, cybersecurity and identity protection, management of information technology, and use of electronic systems.

The bill includes provisions that

  • establish the IRS Independent Office of Appeals to resolve federal tax controversies without litigation;
  • require the IRS to develop comprehensive customer service and IRS personnel training strategies;
  • exempt certain low-income taxpayers from payments required to submit an offer-in-compromise;
  • modify certain tax enforcement procedures and requirements;
  • establish requirements for responding to Taxpayer Advocate Directives;
  • establish a Community Volunteer Income Tax Assistance Matching Grant Program;
  • require the IRS to give public notice of the closure of taxpayer assistance centers;
  • modify procedures for whistle-blowers;
  • establish requirements for cybersecurity and identity protection;
  • provide notification to taxpayers of suspected identity theft;
  • require the appointment of a Chief Information Officer who shall develop and implement a multiyear strategic plan for IRS information technology needs;
  • modify requirements for managing IRS information technology;
  • expand electronic filing of tax returns;
  • prohibit the rehiring of certain IRS employees who were removed for misconduct;
  • require mandatory e-filing by tax-exempt organizations and notice before revocation of tax-exempt status for failure to file; and
  • increase penalties for failure to file tax returns.

The bill also requires the IRS to implement

  • an Internet platform for Form 1099 filings,
  • a fully automated program for disclosing taxpayer information for third-party income verification using the Internet, and
  • uniform standards and procedures for accepting electronic signatures.

summary.headline: The Taxpayer First Act of 2019 changes how the IRS is organized, how it serves taxpayers, how it protects data, and how it handles tax filing rules.
summary.what_it_does: The law creates an independent IRS Office of Appeals to settle tax disputes without going to court. It requires the IRS to build customer service and employee training plans, and to give public notice before closing taxpayer assistance centers. It adds cybersecurity and identity theft protections, including notice to taxpayers when identity theft is suspected, and requires a Chief Information Officer to plan IRS technology needs. It also expands electronic filing, sets new rules for tax-exempt groups, and raises penalties for failing to file returns.

who_it_affects.group: Taxpayers in tax disputes with the IRS
who_it_affects.how: They can have certain disagreements heard by the new independent Office of Appeals instead of going straight to court.

who_it_affects.group: Low-income taxpayers who offer to settle a tax debt
who_it_affects.how: Certain low-income people are exempt from the fee normally required to submit an offer-in-compromise.
The IRS must notify taxpayers when it suspects their identity has been stolen.
They must file electronically and receive notice before losing tax-exempt status for failing to file.

who_it_affects.group: People who fail to file tax returns
who_it_affects.how: Penalties for not filing on time are increased.
A matching grant program is created to support Community Volunteer Income Tax Assistance programs.
Certain employees removed for misconduct cannot be rehired, and the IRS must train staff and plan customer service.

who_it_affects.group: Tax return preparers and businesses that file information returns
who_it_affects.how: The IRS must offer an online platform for Form 1099 filings and accept electronic signatures under uniform standards.
